THE SACRED SCRIPT — A WORLD WHERE EVERYTHING HAS ONE GLORIOUS PURPOSE

Irreverents \| Core creative direction, with clearly marked examples \| 22 November 2026

# CONFIRMED DIRECTION — THE OWNER'S INTENT

The world has essentially made a religion of the Hero's Journey. Its inhabitants have extreme main-quest and main-character syndrome. Everything is part of the main quest; everyone wants everything to fit the EXPECTED GLORIOUS NARRATIVE EXACTLY. Everyone is profoundly typecast. Everything is SO meaningful because everything contributes to the grand story. Everything is FOR EXACTLY WHAT IT APPEARS TO BE FOR.

This is more precise than “a world obsessed with stories.” It is a CULTURE OF UTTER NARRATIVE CONFORMITY: extreme reverence, role fidelity, intentional predictability, and suspicion of improvisation.

The protagonists are the exception. They see a thing and immediately imagine a use that has absolutely nothing to do with its approved glorious significance. Their fixation is concrete, playful, daring and potentially catastrophic. They do not set out to deliver a philosophical critique. They simply cannot resist the much more interesting possibilities in front of them.

The title “Irreverents” is player-facing, not what the heroes call themselves in-world.

# CRITICAL CORRECTION — NOT A SELF-REINTERPRETING FLEXIBLE WORLD

An earlier exploratory notion had every disrupted event seamlessly reclassified as another beat of the Hero's Journey. That should NOT be the default. The owner's clarification makes the culture much more rigid.

When a player suplexes the king through stained glass, most people should NOT serenely announce “Ah, the Crossing of the Threshold.” They should be appalled: the king was supposed to deliver the Call, the heroes were supposed to accept the quest, the guard was supposed to guard, and a throne room is emphatically NOT for suplexing the monarch.

Some priests, chroniclers or enthusiasts might later attempt increasingly strained reinterpretations, but that is a secondary reaction to the crisis, not a magical mechanism that makes everything conform.

The humor and tension arise because the ordinary world desperately wants events to unfold as expected and genuinely DOES NOT KNOW WHAT TO DO when the player finds another use.

# THE WORLD'S THEORY OF EVERYTHING

Every person, artifact, place, task, danger, relationship and inconvenience has a prescribed role in a single glorious story. A village plague is the Call. A tavern meeting is the Encounter. The grumpy old mentor is the Wise Guide. The third locked gate is the Third Trial. The villain has a Final Form, because grand villains should. The blacksmith's sword is forged for the decisive righteous strike.

The world does not think “one of many possible uses.” It thinks “the proper significance and function.”

This worldview can be religious in the strongest sense: sacred story phases, ceremonial language, inherited duties and moral reverence toward correct roles. Whether there is a literal church, deity, scripture, order or cosmology remains OPEN, as are invented names.

# EVERYONE IS EXTREMELY TYPECAST

People behave as characters in their own magnificent story and expect everybody else to behave as the archetype that belongs in that story.

The king is THE KING: grave, ceremonial, concerned about the world, keeper of prophecies, giver of quests. He takes the court so seriously he can speak indefinitely.

The royal champion is THE CHAMPION: honorable, proud of magnificent armor, eager for a fair duel, highly concerned with protocol and reputation.

The wizard is THE WIZARD: cryptic, wise, alchemical, faintly mysterious, waiting to advise the correct heroic moment.

The princess is THE PRINCESS: whatever her culturally prescribed place in the glorious rescue or royal destiny may be, the court wants her to enact it exactly.

The blacksmith is THE BLACKSMITH: prepares The Sword of Destiny for its rightful purpose, not for being thrown through an auction-house window.

The guardian of a temple is THE GUARDIAN: administers the three trials, not a practical suggestion for bypassing the temple entirely.

The dark lord is THE DARK LORD: expects bold declarations, terror, armies, the inevitable showdown, and a worthy hero to oppose him.

The merchant is THE MERCHANT: provides supplies for the hero's journey; the tavern keeper provides rumors; the dragon is a fearsome adversary at the place appointed for dragons.

Each role is lived with fervent sincerity. These are archetypal behavioral proposals, not a finalized cast or requirement to flatten every named character into identical lines.

# EVERY OBJECT HAS AN OFFICIALLY CORRECT PURPOSE

This is a particularly powerful GAMEPLAY principle.

A legendary sword is for slaying the foretold evil.

A sacred key is for opening the sacred door.

A magic cloak awarded for heroism is for safely progressing to the next trial.

A royal carriage is for conveying a dignitary to the necessary ceremony.

A dragon's cage is for safely holding the kingdom's legendary menace.

A champion's armor is for the champion to wear while representing the kingdom.

A memorial hall is for solemnly honoring the properly heroic.

A throne-room stained-glass window is for reminding visitors of the monarchy's historic splendor.

The heroes' different perspective is functional, not merely rhetorical: sword cuts ropes and supports, key opens other opportunities when applicable, cloak enables a heist, carriage becomes a hijacked projectile, dragon cage is opened, champion can be thrown, and throne-room glass becomes an irresistible launch target.

IMPORTANT: “Everything is for exactly what it seems like it's for” describes the WORLD'S EXPECTATIONS and the designers' clear visual signposting, NOT arbitrary engine-enforced single-use objects. The comedy only works because the player can physically use things otherwise.

# MEANING INFLATION

Nothing can be trivial. Every petty inconvenience is heavy with destiny. A lost chicken, a broken cart axle, a missing boot or an unpaid bill must be interpreted as a meaningful stage of the Journey. A person dropping a spoon might apologize for mishandling the Trial of Household Vigilance. There are no socially acceptable “side quests,” because every challenge must be a meaningful part of the heroic sequence.

Do not necessarily make every NPC literally utter jargon constantly. Show it in pompous institutions, ceremony, costumes, architectural hierarchy, repeated staging, NPC confidence, overwrought announcements and players noticing that apparently different regions repeat the same ritual pattern.

Culturally meaningful does NOT equal emotionally satisfying for players. The game provides countless more interesting systems-level distractions.

# THE WORLD IS EXTREMELY PREDICTABLE

At the age-old shrine, three trials await, and everyone knows it. At the forge, the ancient master awaits a chosen hero to grant a unique weapon. A mentor speaks in riddles because mentors do; a villain issues a challenge because villains must; the royal court opens every chapter with solemn exposition.

The predictability should be amusing but also exploitable. Players know the champion will stand politely at the appointed arena, so they can infiltrate his armory while he practices his entrance. Players know that ceremonies will leave certain halls unattended, so they can steal valuables. They know a mentor will deliver a portentous speech at a crossroads; they can sneak into the mentor's cottage while he waits there.

The world should not conceal secret subversions behind every trope; that would weaken the entire premise. More often the trope is played absolutely straight until the PLAYER alters it.

# THE MAIN QUEST VERSUS ACTUAL POSSIBILITY

The official Grand Quest is real, serious, lavishly detailed, all-consuming and everyone else's highest priority. It should be available, but not forced as the player's primary activity. It may itself be mechanically rich, but the party keeps getting drawn to more enticing nearby opportunities.

This must NOT be a standard “main mission plus optional side missions” world whose architecture silently forces linearity. A plot-chosen hero can ignore the Call indefinitely. A difficult boss should not block all other regions. Powers, character recruitment, secrets, heists and escaping impossible pursuits provide alternatives that grow more enticing with time.

# THE THRONE ROOM IS THE PERFECT MICROSCOSM

Opening image: king on throne, champion in beautiful armor, wizard with odd pills, a captive dragon, a suspicious wall, a treasury nearby and a giant stained-glass window.

The king begins the world's most meaningful, carefully structured royal address. The event has a very obvious intended purpose: the heroes listen and embark on the main quest.

The player sees something entirely different: opportunity to pickpocket, befriend the dragon, feed magic pills, steal an artifact, open a secret route, suplex the king or simply flee.

The speech continues indefinitely if left alone. Approximately three hours of uninterrupted listening seamlessly transform into actual end credits. This approved absurd ending dramatizes perfect obedience to the culture's grand storyline: you have completed the game by letting the assigned significance consume the experience.

If the king is attacked, guards are genuinely upset; courtiers are outraged, and the social consequences are real. They do not all applaud the “unexpected chapter.”

# THE WORLD'S RELATIONSHIP WITH THE HEROES

The heroes may perform an expected great deed, and the population adores them because the ordained story has advanced.

Then the heroes take a sacred reward and use it for a spectacular theft. This is not merely criminal; it is a profound category violation. The treasured cloak was GIVEN FOR THE QUEST. People cannot understand why its recipients would use it to rob the same town.

The resulting pursuit can draw them into a dangerous arena, force an alliance against undead gladiators, and produce contradictory gratitude, resentment and awe. Ordinary people still inhabit real lives; they aren't actors who exist solely to maintain the script.

Afterward some officials insist on a glorious interpretation, others demand justice, and locals just want their belongings back. The world may love, fear, hate and depend on the heroes simultaneously.

# THE HALL OF LEGENDS

The confirmed Hall records extraordinary real events—stealth, last stands and escapes—with representative screenshots, statistics and credit to everyone involved. It is a real, attackable, robbable physical location that can memorialize a battle within itself.

A compelling PROPOSED tension: the institution is architecturally and ceremonially organized to honor APPROPRIATE heroic chapters, but its factual records increasingly feature the wrong deeds in the wrong places. The curators are intensely disturbed by being forced to pedestal a legendary heist or the destruction of the museum. The Hall's recognition algorithm stays as impartial as the approved design calls for; the NPCs around it want the record to fit sacred categories.

An encounter at the Hall can create the ultimate paradox: the memorial faithfully celebrates the day the protagonists vandalized the memorial.

# PROPOSED WORLD INSTITUTIONS

The Order of the Call: official messengers who bring heroic quests at prescribed times and are offended when the recipient is eating or stealing a cart.

The Guild of Mentors: formally trains elders to deliver timely, cryptic wisdom; may issue certificates for proper dramatic pacing.

The Royal Bureau of Prophetic Compliance: checks that sacred artifacts reach the right people and that the correct sequence of trials is respected.

The Society of Worthy Adversaries: enemies dedicated to preparing appropriately impressive final confrontations and suitably dramatic entrances.

The Chroniclers' Collegium: writes weighty histories of absolutely everything, and becomes distressed by events that cannot be cleanly classified.

The Hall's Curators: keep a grave record of heroic greatness while coping with deeply unheroic player greatness.

All institutions, titles and mechanics are examples only; the cultural commitment itself is the owner-confirmed direction.

# CHARACTER DESIGN / WRITING RULES

Play archetypes completely straight. They are deeply sincere and certain of their destiny, not ironic meta-joke characters.

Don't give every NPC a secret desire to be a different archetype; that would make the world much less predictably typecast.

NPCs should be allowed to have real emotional stakes, habits and meaningful relationships within their role. Strong typecasting is the shared culture's social expectation, not a ban on all individuality.

Make the best jokes the consequence of actions: the hero uses the king for a wrestling move while the king is still delivering the Call.

Dialogue should express real offense at inappropriate uses, not continuously affirm “everything is part of the plan.”

Let the heroes' physical experiments produce the unexpected; do not substitute a lengthy cutscene mocking conventional narrative.

A thing's intended purpose must be obvious from its design—but not mechanically exclusive.

Keep game-scale pixel environments calm, bright, legible and not overstimulating; solemn architecture can use clear recurring motifs rather than a forest of glowing symbols.

# WHAT REMAINS OPEN

Whether this “religion” has supernatural efficacy, explicit divine entities, a central organization, regional denominations or visible prophecy magic.

Whether the physical world itself is deterministic or only its inhabitants' behavior is predictable. RECOMMENDED DEFAULT: the latter, so player improvisation truly changes events.

Which archetypes become recruitable and whether a few inhabitants resist their roles. Exceptions should be rare and meaningful, not the usual hidden twist.

Names of institutions, king, villain, kingdom, seals and legendary objects.

How the main quest behaves when players kill major story figures, steal major sacred items or leave the story untouched for many hours.

How much the Hall's chroniclers attempt to reframe an incident without compromising the Hall's honest recording.

# VISION ACCEPTANCE TESTS

A first-time player can predict what a mentor, king or temple guardian will say or do within seconds of meeting them.

The world genuinely expects a sacred sword to serve one glorious purpose, but the player can discover other physically valid uses.

Disruption provokes authentic confusion, distress or resistance; it is not universally absorbed as “part of the plan.”

The game does not secretly require the player to pursue the sacred arc.

An improvised player-created moment feels more exciting than the elaborately staged official narrative.

OWNER REFINEMENT — THE WORLD IS DELIGHTED TO PLAY ITS PART (22 NOV 2026)

This is NOT a grim civilization of people secretly trapped in false roles. Everyone is GENUINELY DELIGHTED and PROUD to perform their typecast part in the glorious Hero’s Journey. The storekeeper absolutely loves being a storekeeper; stocking provisions, welcoming travelers, quoting prices, dispensing conventional advice and watching heroes walk out equipped for their destiny is a life's fulfillment. The blacksmith delights in forging the sacred blade. The mentor savors giving cryptic wisdom. The guard enjoys guarding. The champion glories in honorable combat. The dark lord thrills at being a magnificent and appropriately intimidating final adversary. The satisfaction is sincere, not ironic or a mask over latent rebellion.

This reframes any earlier phrases such as “oppressive role expectations,” “a role people secretly wish to escape,” or “narrative tyranny”: those should NOT be the default emotional world. The setting can include hardship and meaningful stakes, but the everyday cultural texture is exuberant, proud, cooperative role fulfillment. Every NPC feels their life has extraordinary purpose precisely because they are playing their part so well. People may congratulate the baker for providing a particularly archetypal loaf or the old sage for delivering a magnificently well-timed riddle; everybody enthusiastically appreciates the predictability.

The protagonists' improvised use of familiar objects doesn't necessarily expose a hidden desire for liberation. It bewilders and can distress people who are otherwise radiantly satisfied. “Why would you turn my shop into a vehicle? It is a SHOP, a beautiful shop, where I sell supplies for the glorious Journey!” The player may delight in the impossible stunt, but the storekeeper remains proud of his vocation and can be furious about harm to it.

Comedy calibration: the main cast is intensely indifferent; the rest of the world is intensely and joyfully earnest. Avoid making NPCs resent their jobs, wink at being game tropes, or assume they are waiting to become subversive. A few exceptions can be developed intentionally, but are not the defining world premise.

Example vignette (illustrative, not locked script): A shopkeeper radiantly announces, “Welcome, noble travelers! Whatever you require for your destined adventure, my shelves are at your service!” The heroes ask whether he can sell them the entire building so they can put wheels on it and use it to breach the royal fortress. The shopkeeper is genuinely perplexed. He loves the shop; he does not want a different life. It has exactly the purpose it is supposed to have.

Gameplay consequence: typecast role-pride supplies dependable routines and expectations that players can learn, respect, exploit or shock. A character whose pride is being an excellent merchant is predictable in how he opens, closes, protects merchandise, responds to shopping and reacts when the purpose of the store is violated. That predictability is useful as physical gameplay information, not just dialogue flavor.

OWNER-APPROVED RESPONSE LOOP — HORROR AT DEVIATION, INSTANT RELIEF AT CONFORMITY (22 NOV 2026)

The inhabitants are not merely upset when heroes do something unexpectedly irreverent. They are ABSOLUTELY HORRIFIED. This is why resistance can become so intense: the heroes are violating what everyone firmly believes each scene, role and artifact is FOR. Conversely, when the heroes begin acting “normally” again, inhabitants pacify unusually fast and are cheerfully certain that all is proceeding as it should: “Yup! Just as expected!” The same predictability that fuels extreme alarm makes de-escalation incredibly rapid.

Social stealth can therefore involve performing the obvious role rather than hiding, and pursuit can be escaped through a convincing return to expected behavior. Distinguish the current emotional reassurance from lingering broken property or historical grievances, without letting those details dilute the sudden reversal. Working mechanic label: Narrative Dissonance. Full system elaboration: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jQssgW8w1oXo_14lLhbGHVwWTPef7y2TEU_aCD_nMvQ/edit

ESCALATION REFINEMENT — OWNER CONFIRMED 22 NOV 2026

Any unexpected behavior is ASSUMED A TEMPORARY FLUKE, because everyone takes the proper Hero's Journey as certain. Persistent deviation creates mounting COGNITIVE DISSONANCE and intense distress; gentle correction turns to urgency, collective resistance, and eventually even shopkeepers, other civilians and pet cats throw themselves at the heroes to stop them and restore the expected story. They are not generally skilled fighters, and in extreme distress may abandon their beloved role to defend the script itself. The reversal is equally dramatic: convincing normal behavior can rapidly reassure them that everything is once again just as expected, so people quickly resume proud, delighted routine. This is not a conventional law-enforcement wanted system. Detailed system addendum: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jQssgW8w1oXo_14lLhbGHVwWTPef7y2TEU_aCD_nMvQ/edit

THREE-MODE NPC RULE — OWNER CONFIRMED (22 NOV 2026)

Every inhabitant (including villains) generally occupies one of three modes: BUSINESS AS USUAL, CONFUSION / DISTRESS, and ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE. Business as usual means the script is recognizable—not that everyone is calm or good. A shopkeeper feels perfectly fulfilled heroically resisting a villain's expected robbery, but is horrified if that same villain walks in politely to buy a potion. Even villainy is a beloved narrative vocation. Villains also enter distress/rage when expected heroes refuse to behave like heroic adversaries. Persistence in unexpected behavior can drive everyone to fury; reestablishing the expected scene restores joyful certainty quickly. See core NPC mechanics: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wuGuCu1RhXXhdWuU55ZcJJ8rZAbCx98mZfdqsyrgMv8/edit
